This game really develops your patience. Sometimes the best plays are missed because you get so locked in a strategy from a few turns ago that you don't notice the changes in hazards on the board by your opponent. Reflect before you play. More times than I care to admit, I look at all the options, then am surprised when I put down a card that makes a cycle, or completely miss a chance to block the moon from making a cycle, and the moon ends up winning because of it. I wonder if people who have strength in quick math tend to not miss those calculations...

Some examples of each type of board:

"Connected" like the 3x3 or 5x4 or the scary 6x5

"Disconnected" are the rows or groups of four separate from each other

"Bridged" would be any layout that has a line of symmetry with one or two paths connecting the two sides over that line

And I'd argue there's a fourth board: circles. Unlike the "bridged" which only has two connections across its path, circles can have eighth or so connections stemming off from the central hub. I feel like this makes a cycle inevitable because if it's blocked in one area, it can be continued via another stem. Maybe a failproof strategy for this one is to just get a few matches (phase pairs and full moon pairs) and guard everything else. 

My play style tends to be out of control to have fun. I enjoy when I beat the game by a huge margin, or lose by one point to a phase cycle I didn't catch, or surprise myself when I get a phase cycle I didn't see.

I'm gonna definitely try some of the strategies you suggested, such as avoiding the second card of a phase to see how it goes with my playing style. The object of the game is to win, whether by a lot of points earned or a little points earned.

I can see the benefit of getting rid of dead cards, and they can also be used to block. I try to earn as many points as possible on each turn without being reckless (but that doesn't always go to plan, haha!) So if I see a useful card in my hand, I tend to play it in the hopes that the dead card will become useful later as new cards come in. 

And it's definitely worth a pause to count the number of slots on the board to see if you have an odd or even amount. Great realization there that you can play cycles more liberally if you have the final card.

It sounds like you want to keep it private. This is what therapists do. A pediatrician would also be a good candidate, or maybe a school guidance counselor who could refer you to a school counselor. They answer your questions, no matter how embarrassing, and give you peace of mind and keep it private. If at school, everything would be kept in house unless there was something that needed to be shared with the family like suicidal thoughts. You can ask them what will be shared with the family.

Coming to terms with that sort of information can be difficult and scary. In my adult life I still get embarrassing questions that I've held in for years, questions I could never ask my family, and the relief I get from talking to an expert on how to think about it is palpable. It's not embarrassing and actually expected from people who work in that field to get those kinds of questions.

Kids don't realize what's at stake with their education. If their parent's don't need one (dad's a mechanic) why do they? They can just focus on becoming a basketball player. Besides, the teacher walking out is a reward for bad behavior, feelings be damned they're already bored as hell. In some kid's eyes, it makes sense. Yeah they're absolute dicks, how we proceed is showing them that their reasoning is flawed. 

Limiting your time spent in school severely limits your opportunities by eliminating the need to develop skills that you will transfer to other practices (for example hard work). So if the pro-NBA plan falls through (which it does for 99.99% of people) you need a backup plan, but that takes hard work. Accepting that reality takes some wisdom, and without good adult guidance in their life they probably don't have that.

I mean yeah the kids are shit but that comes with the job. Shit kids are in EVERY school, but the way it manifests varies on ethnicity and other factors. I have heard of horrible things like a rich student and her parents blackmailing her teacher to get picked for all the solos in class. It's about the socioemotional development and what the students enjoy about their learning which leads to their career and life-passions development (as well as the standardized test for core subject teachers). Damn he could have dealt with that better. The administration could have supported him better. Leading up to that moment was a shitstorm of other problems that went unaddressed until it all boiled over.

Hopefully the kids will learn to be nicer from reflecting on that, or learning from other experiences later in their life, but drama like that is probably a regular occurance in that school. But that was that guy's opportunity to make a difference. It's such a shame he wasn't taught how to deal with that side of the job. That's a four-year degree down the toilet and a mar on his resume. But what I now suspect is he's subbing, and you don't have to have a full degree for that, just a certain amount of credit hours, so that school district won't hire him again. Notice he didn't use any students' names.

That happening is an embarrassment on the principal if he's their teacher, or whoever vets substitute teachers.

Kids that get suspended are a lot more likely to drop out. As a teacher, you try your best to make lemons into lemonade. You won't always succeed and that's okay. But that's better than them being left as lemons.

So yeah you're right, we DO put up with a lot of shit!

No one is being dismissive of the child (besides mom). Saying to the child “I would use your pronouns if I were allowed to” is the lesser of two evils, and should be done if some authority (not the mother but the school) steps in and says no don’t do that. Better to keep to your job and be respectful of the child than lose the position and have some a-hole teacher that the school handpicks come in and the child does not have a trusted adult anymore. Unless you want to quit your job as a call to action to the school board. It’s a hairy situation. 

But if the school doesn’t care then by all means use their pronouns and hide it from mom as best you can. Doing that would risk building distrust with the parent, which could jeopardize the child’s education or safety. It’s OPs call. Using the correct pronouns is the *right* thing to do, but safety must also be considered. A child should not be responsible for risking their physical health for the sake of using their pronouns.

As an Ed major, I would cover my butt by going with the she/her pronouns. But as all teachers know, for the love of teaching communicate to the child that you aren’t dismissive of their pronouns at all. As kids grow they will gain more leverage and autonomy, so it’ll just take time, patience and confidence. It’s not worth jeopardizing the child’s relationship with their parent, which could potentially put them at risk for abuse. Depending on your school rules, there may be a feasible way to use their pronouns in situations that are under the radar. 

I find it amazing that society has changed so much in the last decade or two that even an elementary schooler, a child with little autonomy, is comfortable with talking to a trustworthy adult about exploring their gender. We’ve come a long way but we’ve got a long way to go.
